distribution: Wild in the Appalachians and the Ozarks, from southern Pennsylvania to Georgia and Arkansas.

habitat: Dry hillsides and open woods. Planted widely as a street tree, it does best in full sun but stands almost any soil, even very dry ones, and seeds itself freely.
distribution: Wild in China, Korea and Manchuria, and naturalized in Japan since at least the 1200s. Brought to North America in 1763, it is invasive in some southern states.

habitat: A cool, moist climate with 36 to 52 inches of rain a year, deep winter snow and only 90 to 150 frost-free days, on mountain slopes and in cool lowlands. In Vermont it is the spruce of the Green Mountains.
distribution: From the Maritime Provinces west to Maine, southern Quebec and southeastern Ontario, and south into New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Massachusetts; and along the high Appalachians through western Maryland, West Virginia and Virginia to western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: River valleys in warm temperate and Mediterranean country where the ground stays moist. A fast-growing tree that needs light, it colonizes woodland edges, meadows, wetlands and riverbanks, and grows almost anywhere, wet or dry, acid or strongly alkaline, if only as a shrub at the extremes. Long planted in North America, it spreads by root suckers.
distribution: Native to the riverside and coastal forests of central and southern Europe, from North Africa to Poland and from Spain to western Siberia and Central Asia. Brought to the United States in the 1700s as a shade tree, it has naturalized in many places and become invasive in some.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Dry, poor, rocky or sandy uplands, in climates from the humid East, with over 60 inches of rain a year, to the semiarid edge of the plains in Texas, with 22. It grows in pure stands in the Cross Timbers, the belt where the forest gives way to prairie in central Oklahoma and Texas.
distribution: From southeastern Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut and Long Island west through Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to southeastern Iowa and Missouri; south to eastern Kansas, western Oklahoma and central Texas; and east to central Florida. It is large and abundant on the southern coastal plain, the Piedmont and the lower Appalachian slopes.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A cultivated tree; planted, it wants full sun and acid to neutral soil. Its seeds and wilted leaves are poisonous if eaten in quantity.
distribution: Domesticated in China several thousand years ago from wild trees of northwest China; the name persica comes from its arrival in Europe by way of Persia.

habitat: Riverbanks in dry country; planted, it takes almost any soil, even standing water. Most weeping willows planted in the North are its hardier hybrids.
distribution: Wild in dry parts of northern China, Korea, Mongolia, Japan and Siberia. Grown for millennia across Asia, it reached Europe along the Silk Road.

habitat: Hill forests. Planted in the eastern United States as a street tree and for wildlife, it has escaped into forests and is now considered a noxious weed in places. It wants full sun and acid soil.
distribution: Wild across eastern Asia, from the Himalayas to China, Korea and Japan.

habitat: Thickets and woodland edges. Its purple-leaved selections are common street trees, short-lived and brittle, doing best in sun or part shade on moist, well-drained, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild in southeastern Europe and western Asia, from the Balkans to the Caucasus and Central Asia.

habitat: The understory of moist, rich woods and ravines, in shade or dappled light, spreading by suckers into colonies.
distribution: Wild only in a small area of the Southeast, mostly in Alabama, with smaller stands in neighboring states.

habitat: The understory of moist woods and streamsides, on the coastal plain and in the Piedmont. Planted, it does best in part shade.
distribution: Wild across the southeastern United States, from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas.

habitat: Bogs, wet woods and dry rocky ground alike; it spreads by suckers into thickets. Planted, it takes sun or part shade and almost any soil, wet or dry.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and south to the Appalachians. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Where it has escaped: woods, old fields and edges, in sun or shade, on almost any soil, even very dry ones. Planted widely as a hedge, it is now banned from sale in several states as invasive.
distribution: Wild in Japan and eastern China; escaped across the Northeast, Vermont included.

habitat: Shady woods, streamsides and wooded hillsides. Planted, it grows in anything from deep shade to full sun, on almost any soil, and stands occasional flooding or drought.
distribution: Wild in the southeastern United States, from Virginia to Florida and west to Mississippi.

habitat: Swamps, pond edges and streams, often standing in water. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in acid soil that stays wet.
distribution: Wild across eastern and southern North America, from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to California, and on into Central America and Cuba. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Dry steppe and riverbanks. Hardy enough to be planted across the Canadian Prairies from the 1880s for shelterbelts and windbreaks, it fixes nitrogen and has escaped in places.
distribution: Wild in Siberia, Mongolia and northern China.

habitat: Thickets, old fields, roadsides, meadows, woodland edges and riverbanks, spreading by underground stems into clumps. Planted, it grows in anything from deep shade to full sun, on almost any soil, wet or dry.
distribution: Wild across northeastern North America, from Maine and southern Quebec to Minnesota and south to Virginia and Oklahoma. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Wet thickets, swamps, bogs and streamsides. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist soil, and stands occasional flooding.
distribution: Wild across most of northern North America, from Newfoundland to Alaska and south in the mountains. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Exposed, rocky ground and open woods, in cool climates, on dry or infertile soils; it grows in sun or shade alike.
distribution: Wild across northeastern North America, from Newfoundland to Saskatchewan and south in the Appalachians. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Thickets and open woods; where it has escaped, the understory of woods, in sun or shade, on almost any soil. Planted widely for its red fall color, it is banned from sale in several states, Vermont among them.
distribution: Wild in northeastern China, Korea and Japan; escaped across the eastern United States.

habitat: Woods, dry ridges and stream banks. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in acid soil.
distribution: Wild only in the southern Appalachians, from North Carolina to Alabama.

habitat: Moist or rocky wooded slopes, ravines, stream banks and the foot of bluffs, mostly in shade. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild across the eastern United States, from New York to Florida and west to Oklahoma.

habitat: Moist woods, stream banks, wooded slopes and bluffs, often over limestone. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in the southeastern United States, from Tennessee and North Carolina to Florida and Louisiana.

habitat: Swamps, wet thickets and pond shores; a deciduous holly, whose red berries feed birds into winter. Planted, it grows in anything from shade to full sun, in moist, acid soil.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and south to Florida. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Moist woods, swamps, wet pine barrens and streamsides. Planted, it does best in part shade or dappled light, in moist soil, even standing water.
distribution: Wild in the southeastern United States, from New Jersey to Florida and west to Missouri, Louisiana and eastern Texas.

habitat: Dry, rocky, open ground and old pastures. It varies from a small tree to a low, often sprawling shrub in exposed places.
distribution: The most widespread conifer in the world, wild across the cool parts of North America, Europe and Asia. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Mountain thickets and streamsides, forming broad, dense clumps of arching stems. Planted, it does best in part shade, dappled light or even deep shade, on well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild from central and southern China to southern Korea and Japan.

habitat: Planted for wildlife and hedges, it has escaped into woods, edges and fields, in anything from deep shade to full sun, and become one of the worst invasive shrubs of eastern forests.
distribution: Native to eastern Asia: northeastern China, Korea and the Russian Far East. Naturalized across much of the eastern United States.

habitat: Hedgerows and woodlands, especially on chalk, in sun or part shade; in Britain it is the only native privet. Planted for hedges, it has escaped in the eastern United States.
distribution: Wild across Europe and into North Africa and western Asia.

habitat: It climbs trees, walls and rocks or sprawls over the ground at woodland edges and in thickets, in sun, part shade or dappled light, on almost any soil.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from southern Canada to Florida and west to Texas, and south into Mexico. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Stream banks, rocky slopes and woodland edges. Planted, it does well in sun or part shade, on almost any well-drained soil, moist or dry.
distribution: Wild across much of eastern and central North America, from Quebec to Minnesota and south to Georgia. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Woodland edges, ravines, slopes, open fields and fencerows, where it forms dense thickets. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild across most of North America, from Newfoundland to British Columbia and south to North Carolina and California. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Dry, open ground: woodland edges, old fields, roadsides and railroad banks, and also stream and swamp margins, spreading by seed and root suckers into thickets. Planted, it wants full sun and well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Minnesota and south in the Appalachians. Native to Vermont.

habitat: A light-hungry pine of rock: fissured bedrock, boulder fields, alluvial fans and even sand dunes, on poor, free-draining ground over almost any rock, from limestone to granite; it also takes nutrient-poor raised bogs. In high mountains it forms dense, low thickets near the tree line.
distribution: The mountains of central and southern Europe, the Alps, Pyrenees, Carpathians and Balkans, with outlying stands in Spain's mountains and in bogs north of the Alps.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Wooded slopes and ridges, high mountain balds and rocky slopes, and down along streams, often in dense thickets. Planted, it grows in shade or sun, in moist, well-drained, acid soil.
distribution: Wild in the southern Appalachians, from Virginia to Georgia.

habitat: Dry, rocky slopes and open woods, where it spreads by root suckers into low colonies and thickets. Planted, it does well in sun or part shade, in acid soil.
distribution: Wild across much of eastern and central North America, from Vermont and Ontario to Florida and west to the Plains.

habitat: Brought from Asia as a rootstock for garden roses, and later planted for living fences and erosion control, it has become an invasive thicket-former in fields, pastures and woods.
distribution: Wild in eastern China, Korea and Japan; escaped across the eastern United States, Vermont included.

habitat: Moist ground along streams and marshes, wet thickets, moist forests, disturbed ground and roadsides. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Manitoba and south to Florida and Texas, and on into Central and South America. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Woods and thickets in low mountains, where it trails over the ground and climbs trees. It grows in sun or shade on almost any soil, even very dry ones, and has escaped from gardens to become invasive.
distribution: Wild in China, Korea, Japan and the Philippines; escaped in the eastern United States.

habitat: Wet savannas, pocosins, bay swamps, bogs and the edges of swamps on the coastal plain. Planted, it does well in sun, part shade or dappled light, in acid soil.
distribution: Wild on the southeastern coastal plain, from North Carolina to Alabama.

habitat: Mountain forest edges and thickets. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild in eastern and southern China, Japan, Taiwan, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands.

habitat: Pine barrens, bogs and wet sandy woods; an evergreen holly. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, acid soil.
distribution: Wild on the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, from Nova Scotia to Florida and Louisiana.

habitat: Rocky shores, cliffs, dunes and sandy barrens, hugging the ground. Planted, it wants full sun and well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild throughout Canada and Alaska and across the northern United States from Maine to Montana.

habitat: It climbs cliffs, rocks and trees by tendrils tipped with sticky discs. Planted, it grows in sun or part shade on almost any well-drained soil, and covers walls.
distribution: Wild in Japan, Korea and eastern China.

habitat: Mountain slopes and thickets. It escapes readily from gardens into woods, fields and roadsides, in sun or part shade.
distribution: Wild in Japan, Korea and China; naturalized, and invasive, in parts of the eastern United States.

habitat: Nutrient-rich bottomlands, woodland thickets and moist ground along streams, where it spreads by suckers into dense colonies. Planted, it does well in sun or part shade, on moist, well-drained soil, and stands occasional flooding or drought.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from southern Ontario and southwestern Quebec west to Nebraska and Arkansas and south to Florida.

habitat: Still-water swamps, cypress domes, bayous and lake edges. Planted, it wants full sun and acid soil, and grows in standing water or on ordinary moist ground.
distribution: Wild on the southeastern coastal plain, from Virginia to Florida and Louisiana.

habitat: The understory of beech and oak woods, often on chalk and limestone, best in mild oceanic climates. Cold and waterlogging hold it back in the north, drought and heat in the south, where it keeps to higher, north-facing slopes. Some churchyard yews in Britain are reckoned well over a thousand years old.
distribution: Most of Europe, north to Britain, Ireland and southern Scandinavia, the Atlas Mountains of northwest Africa, and Asia Minor; the range map also shows it in the Caucasus and northern Iran. Yew is thought to be the oldest tree genus in Europe.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Bogs, swamps, wet woods and, in the mountains, high-elevation forests. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, acid soil.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Ontario east to Nova Scotia and south to Florida and eastern Texas. The parent of the cultivated blueberry; native to Vermont.

habitat: Moist woods, thickets and stream banks. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild across the eastern United States and Canada, from Maine south to northern Florida and eastern Texas. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Moist ground with rich loam or clay-loam soil, in low woods, swamp borders and along streams, though it also takes drier sites, woodland edges and fencerows; it spreads by suckers.
distribution: Wild in southern Canada from New Brunswick westward, and in the northeastern and midwestern United States. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Dry woods, thickets and roadsides, spreading by suckers; a valuable plant for wildlife. Planted, it does well in sun or part shade on almost any well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in eastern North America, from Connecticut west to eastern Kansas and south to Alabama and Texas.

habitat: Mountain slopes and thickets. Planted, it does best in sun, part shade or dappled light, in moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in northern China, Korea and Japan.

habitat: Rich, moist, shady hardwood forest. Planted, it wants shade or dappled light and moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Quebec to Georgia and west to Minnesota and Oklahoma. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Moist woods, bottomland forests, bogs and swamp edges, often spreading into large colonies, in acid soil.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Georgia and west to Ontario and Arkansas. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Moist, shady woods, thickets and streamsides; very cold-tolerant. Planted, it wants shade or dappled light and moist, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild across much of the Northern Hemisphere, in Europe, Asia and North America. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Damp meadows and riverbanks. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, acid to neutral soil, and stands occasional wet spells.
distribution: Wild from central and eastern Europe to Siberia and Central Asia.

habitat: River floodplains, swampy ground, thickets and the understory of moist woods. Its young coiled fronds are the fiddleheads gathered in Vermont each spring.
distribution: Wild across the cool parts of the Northern Hemisphere.

habitat: Shaded woodland slopes, in moist, well-drained, acid soil. Its fronds stay green all winter.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas, and into northeastern Mexico. Native to Vermont.

habitat: A garden shrub. Planted, it wants full sun and well-drained soil, and does best in moist, rich loam.
distribution: A garden hybrid, not found wild: raised by Niels Hansen in South Dakota from the western sand cherry, Prunus pumila, and the purple-leaved cherry plum.

habitat: A garden shrub, combining the ornamental qualities of English yew with the winter hardiness of Japanese yew. Planted, it grows in sun or part shade, on well-drained soil.
distribution: A garden hybrid of English and Japanese yew, first raised about 1900 by T. D. Hatfield on the Hunnewell estate in Wellesley, Massachusetts. Not found wild.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; NC State Extension

habitat: Moist mountain forests. Planted, it wants full sun and well-drained, acid to neutral soil, and stands some dryness.
distribution: Wild in the mountains of the Caucasus and northeastern Turkey.

habitat: Dry, rocky slopes and ridges, in a continental climate of little precipitation, low humidity and wide swings of temperature. In the north of its range it grows near the lower tree line and on dry sites; farther south it grows both low and high, up to the tree line.
distribution: From Alberta and southeastern British Columbia south through the Rocky Mountains and the Great Basin to New Mexico, Arizona and eastern California, with outlying stands in the western Dakotas and Nebraska, eastern Oregon and southwestern California.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Sandhills, dry hammocks and other dry, sandy, well-drained ground, in a warm climate with 49 to 59 inches of rain a year and occasional summer or fall droughts of one to three months. It grows fast and is short-lived for an oak.
distribution: The Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains from southeastern Virginia to southern Florida and west to southeastern Texas, with a few outlying stands farther north. It grows largest, and most commonly, in north Florida and Georgia.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Rich, moist mountain coves and river valleys, in climates from 39 inches of rain a year in southern Ohio and Illinois to 84 in the North Carolina mountains. The largest of the buckeyes.
distribution: From the mountains of southwestern Pennsylvania down the Ohio valley to extreme southeastern Illinois; south through Kentucky and Tennessee to northern Alabama; east to northern Georgia and northwestern South Carolina; and north through western Virginia and West Virginia.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Dry ridges and slopes in oak-hickory forest, in warm, humid climates averaging 59°F and 53 inches of rain a year, mostly at moderate elevations, around 700 feet and up to about 3,900.
distribution: Broadly across the eastern United States, most abundant in the Appalachians and the Ozarks: north into New England, Vermont included, west to eastern Oklahoma and Texas, and south to Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and the Florida panhandle. It is sparse in the lower Mississippi valley.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Forests, forest edges and mountain slopes. Its fruit is used in traditional Chinese medicine. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid soil.
distribution: Native to China, in the north-central and southeastern provinces. Sources disagree on whether it is also native to Korea and Japan, where it has long been grown.

habitat: Mostly dry limestone uplands. Its four-angled, winged twigs give it the name quadrangulata. Planted, it wants full sun and stands dry spells, on almost any well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in the Midwest and upper South, from southern Michigan and Ontario to Tennessee and Oklahoma.

habitat: Deep, rich, moist bottomland soils, often in the great river swamps, in climates with 150 to 210 frost-free days and 30 to 59 inches of rain a year. Its nuts are the largest of any hickory.
distribution: Widely distributed but nowhere common, from western New York through southern Michigan to southeastern Iowa, south through eastern Kansas into northern Oklahoma, and east through Tennessee into Pennsylvania. It is most prominent in the lower Ohio valley and down the Mississippi to central Arkansas.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Freshwater swamps, bogs and wet ground, sometimes on sandy soils, in a humid climate with 40 to 64 inches of rain spread through the year; it stands winters to −36°F in Maine. Suitable sites are scarce, so its stands are patchy.
distribution: A narrow coastal belt 50 to 130 miles wide from southern Maine to northern Florida and west to southern Mississippi. It matters most in southeastern New Jersey, southeastern Virginia, eastern North Carolina and northwestern Florida.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Rocky slopes and open woods. Most planted junipers of this name are its cultivars, which want well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in eastern Asia: China, Mongolia, Korea, Japan, the Himalayas, Myanmar and the Russian Far East.

habitat: Woods, forest edges and clearings, spreading by suckers. Planted, it does well in sun or part shade, on moist soil, and stands occasional wet spells.
distribution: Wild across the eastern United States, from New York to Florida and west to Missouri and Texas.

habitat: Wooded slopes, cliffs and bluffs, open and rocky woods, limestone glades and riverbanks. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from New Brunswick to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas.

habitat: Open woods, forest edges, streamsides and thickets. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, on almost any well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in the eastern United States and southern Ontario, from New York to Wisconsin and south to Alabama.

habitat: Mountain forests and thickets. Planted, it does well in sun, part shade or dappled light, in moist, well-drained, acid soil.
distribution: Wild in China, Korea, Japan and Taiwan.

habitat: Stream bottoms, valleys and mountain slopes, on a wide variety of sites, in climates from 14 inches of precipitation a year in the Blue Mountains of eastern Oregon to over 100 on Vancouver Island, most of it falling in winter.
distribution: The northwestern United States and southern British Columbia: in the Pacific region from Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland through the valleys of western Washington and Oregon to Sonoma County, California, and inland to Idaho and western Montana.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A light-demanding pioneer of mountain and subalpine country, it needs light at every stage, colonizing ground opened by avalanches, landslides and grazing and forming open woodland. In the Alps and the Tatras it grows in a continental climate of cold, dry, snowy winters; in Poland and the Sudetes, lower down in a milder one.
distribution: Scattered through the mountains of southern, central and eastern Europe, from southeastern France and northern Italy to eastern Poland and central Romania, forming forests from about 600 feet in Poland to 8,200 feet in the Alps.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Moist woods and streamsides in warm temperate to semitropical climates, with at least 210 frost-free days; within its natural range temperatures below 15°F are rare.
distribution: From eastern North Carolina south along the Atlantic coast to the Peace River in central Florida, then west through the southern halves of Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi and across Louisiana into southeastern Texas. It is most common in Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Forest edges and clearings, where it grows fast into thickets of spiny stems. Brought to the United States from eastern Asia in 1830, it has escaped from gardens and is listed as invasive in North Carolina.
distribution: Wild in Japan, Korea, northeastern China and the Russian Far East; escaped in parts of the eastern United States.

habitat: River floodplains in a humid climate with 30 to 79 inches of rain a year, at least 20 of them in the growing season; winter lows can reach −20°F.
distribution: Principally the lower Mississippi valley, west to eastern Kansas and central Texas and east to western Mississippi and Tennessee, with sparse stands from southwestern Ohio to Kentucky and Alabama. It also grows locally in northeastern and central Mexico.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Streamsides and forest edges, in cool-summer climates; it is one of the hardiest maples. Planted, it grows in sun, part shade or dappled light, on almost any well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in northeastern Asia, from Mongolia and Manchuria to Korea and Japan. Invasive in parts of the northern United States.

habitat: Mostly moist woods. Unlike most hawthorns it resists leaf rust; planted, it wants full sun.
distribution: Wild in the southeastern United States.

habitat: Mountain forests of the Caspian coast. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid soil.
distribution: Wild only in the Caspian region of northern Iran and southeastern Azerbaijan, in the Alborz mountains.

habitat: Dry, rocky slopes and ridges in a mostly dry, subhumid climate, though its range reaches from maritime to subalpine to semiarid; it stands −35 to 110°F, but does best where winter lows stay above about −10°F.
distribution: The most widespread tree juniper of western North America, scattered from central British Columbia and southern Alberta through Montana and Idaho to Colorado and northern New Mexico, mostly following the Rocky Mountains, and across the Great Basin to Arizona.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Streamsides and mountain valleys; a common subject for bonsai. Planted, it wants full sun and acid to neutral soil, and stands both wet and dry spells.
distribution: Wild in eastern China and Taiwan; long planted in Japan.

habitat: Mountain forests with warm, dry summers and cool, moist winters, the higher stands blanketed in heavy snow. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in well-drained soil. Its blue-needled form is the usual planted one.
distribution: Wild only in the Atlas and Rif mountains of Morocco and the Tell Atlas of Algeria.

habitat: Mountain forests, pure or mixed with Cilician fir, black pine, Turkish pine and junipers. Planted, it wants full sun and well-drained soil, and stands some dryness.
distribution: Wild in the mountains of Lebanon, Syria and southern Turkey; the cedar on the Lebanese flag. A close relative in the Troodos Mountains of Cyprus, sometimes counted as the same species, is mapped with it.

habitat: Steep, often rocky slopes facing north, east or west, mostly on limestone but also on serpentine, between about 2,600 and 4,900 feet, in closed forest with Norway spruce and black pine higher up and beech lower down; a relic of a once wider range.
distribution: Wild only along the Drina River on the border of Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a total area of only about 1.5 square miles; the main stands are protected in Serbia's Tara Mountains national park.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: The upper subalpine forest near the tree line, where it grows slowly and lives for centuries. A relic of the ice ages, close kin of the Siberian pine, it was pushed into scattered mountain refuges as the climate warmed and Norway spruce outcompeted it.
distribution: The Alps, from the Maritime Alps in France to the Julian Alps in Slovenia, most abundant in the east, with isolated groups in the Tatras, the Carpathians and the Transylvanian Alps.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Rocky mountain ridges and slopes. Planted, it does best in cooler climates on well-drained soil, and suffers in the heat and humidity of the Deep South. Much grown as bonsai.
distribution: Wild in the mountains of Japan.

habitat: Woodlands, thickets and open hillsides. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in well-drained, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild in central and southern China.

habitat: A garden tree. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained soil, acid or alkaline.
distribution: A hybrid of horse chestnut and red buckeye of uncertain origin, which appeared in Europe, probably in Germany, around 1812 to 1818. Not found wild.

habitat: Bottomland and streamsides in a humid, temperate climate of long, hot summers and short, mild winters, with 180 to 300 frost-free days.
distribution: Mainly the bottomlands of the coastal plain from New Jersey and southeastern Pennsylvania south to Georgia and northern Florida and west to eastern Texas, and north up the Mississippi valley to southeastern Oklahoma, Arkansas, southeastern Missouri, southern Illinois, Kentucky and western Tennessee.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mostly dry limestone soils and rocky slopes, in a humid climate, drier on its southwestern fringe, with 120 frost-free days in Vermont to 240 in Texas.
distribution: From western Vermont and New York west through southern Ontario, Michigan and Wisconsin to southeastern Minnesota and Iowa; south to southeastern Nebraska, eastern Kansas, western Oklahoma and central Texas; east to northwestern Florida; and north, mostly in the mountains, to Pennsylvania and southwestern Massachusetts. Local stands grow in the mountains of southeastern New Mexico and Trans-Pecos Texas.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Thickets, streamsides, fencerows, woodlands, pastures and old farms, on rocky or sandy soil, spreading by suckers into thickets. Planted, it does well in sun or part shade, on moist to dry, well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild across most of the eastern and central United States, from New England to Montana and south to Florida and Texas.

habitat: Riverbanks and open woods. It flowers and fruits in late summer, unlike most elms. Planted, it grows fast in sun or part shade, on almost any well-drained soil, and tolerates moist sites.
distribution: Wild in China, Korea, Japan and Taiwan.

habitat: Wild only where both its parents grow; easily propagated, it is the commonest linden of avenues and city streets. The Malmvik lime in Stockholm was planted as a sapling in 1618.
distribution: A natural hybrid of small-leaved and large-leaved linden, found wild at scattered places in Europe wherever the two parents are both native.

habitat: Planted for its early, star-shaped white flowers, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid to neutral soil, and stands occasional wet spells.
distribution: Native to Japan, and planted far beyond it.

habitat: A garden tree. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: A garden hybrid of Kobus and star magnolia, raised by Max Löbner near Dresden shortly before the First World War. Not found wild.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; NC State Extension

habitat: The commonest magnolia of northern gardens, a tree or large shrub with fleshy roots that need room. Planted, it does best with steady moisture in well-drained soil.
distribution: A garden hybrid of the Yulan and lily magnolias, raised in France by Étienne Soulange-Bodin in the 1820s. Not found wild.

habitat: The cherry of the Washington Tidal Basin, and a good small street tree. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: A hybrid that arose in cultivation in Japan, most likely from Edo higan and Oshima cherry, though its parentage is uncertain. Not found wild.

habitat: Long grown in Japanese gardens and at temples, its weeping form since at least the Heian period.
distribution: Whether it was ever a wild species is unclear. Now often classed as Prunus itosakura.
Of obscure origin, probably an old Japanese garden hybrid; it reached Europe from Japan through Siebold in the 1860s.

habitat: Charles Sprague Sargent found it in 1892 in a brackish marsh in Hokkaido. Planted, it wants full sun and well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in Japan. Sargent sent seed to the Arnold Arboretum, which is how it reached gardens.

habitat: A garden shrub. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, fertile, well-drained, acid soil.
distribution: A garden hybrid of Japanese and Chinese witch hazel that arose at the Arnold Arboretum in the 1920s and was named there in 1945. Not found wild.

habitat: It tolerates city air and pollution, which made it the classic street tree of London. Planted, it wants full sun and takes almost any soil, and occasional wet spells.
distribution: A hybrid of the American sycamore and the Oriental plane, which arose in cultivation in Europe. Not found wild.

habitat: Rocky mountain slopes. Planted at temples in Beijing for centuries for its white, flaking bark. In gardens it wants full sun and moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in the mountains of central China, from Shanxi and Hebei to Sichuan.

habitat: Limestone ridges up to the tree line. Planted, it wants full sun and well-drained soil, and does best in cool-summer climates, not in hot, humid ones.
distribution: Wild in the mountains of the Balkans and southern Italy.

habitat: Thickets and mixed woods on hillsides. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in loose, well-drained, neutral soil.
distribution: Wild in northern China.

habitat: Mixed forest on hills and in valleys. Planted, it stands heat and drought once established, on average, well-drained soil in sun or part shade.
distribution: Wild in northern China and Korea.

habitat: Close to streams and rivers, in moist woods. It is an endangered species in the wild, confined to scattered places.
distribution: Wild in Japan, in Hokkaido and Honshu.

habitat: Woodland edges and open woods. Closely related to the Callery pear, and sometimes treated as a variety of it.
distribution: Wild in North and South Korea.

habitat: A cold-hardy garden shrub. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid soil.
distribution: A garden hybrid of English holly and the hardy East Asian Ilex rugosa, raised by Kathleen Meserve at St. James, on Long Island. Not found wild.

habitat: Mountain forests. Most planted ones are dwarf or threadleaf cultivars, which want moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild in central and southern Japan.

habitat: Long cultivated for its bark, used in traditional Chinese medicine; considered threatened in the wild. The only living member of its family. Planted, it wants full sun.
distribution: Native to central China, though whether any truly wild trees remain is doubtful.

habitat: Mixed forest on mountain slopes. The smallest of the lindens, it grows slowly; planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil.
distribution: Wild in northern China and Mongolia.

habitat: Moist, well-drained bottomland and limestone slopes, in a humid, temperate climate of hot summers and short, mild winters, with 45 to 55 inches of rain a year.
distribution: The Atlantic coastal plain from North Carolina to northern Florida and west to central Texas, and north up the Mississippi valley to central Oklahoma, eastern Kansas, Missouri, southern Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Kentucky and Tennessee, with local stands as far north as southern Michigan, Pennsylvania and Maryland.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: The wetter sites of bottomland: swamps and floodplains, in a warm, humid climate with 45 to 60 inches of rain a year and little snow.
distribution: The coastal plain bottomlands from Delaware and Maryland south to Georgia and northwestern Florida and west to eastern Texas, and north up the Mississippi valley to southeastern Oklahoma, Missouri, southern Illinois, southwestern Indiana and western Kentucky.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A garden tree, which wants moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: A hybrid of the yellow, Ohio and red buckeyes that appeared on its own at the Arnold Arboretum in Boston, and was first described there in 1924. Not found wild.
source: Plants of the World Online (Kew); NC State Extension

distribution: A dwarf garden selection of cotoneaster, not found wild. Most cotoneasters grow wild in the mountains of China and the Himalayas.
A weeping garden cherry raised in a nursery, not found wild. Flowering cherries of its kind come from Japan.

habitat: A fast-growing garden tree, much planted as a hedge and screen. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, on almost any well-drained soil.
distribution: A garden hybrid of western redcedar and Japanese arborvitae, not found wild: raised in Denmark in the 1930s and brought to the United States in 1967 by the U.S. National Arboretum. Its western parent grows wild in the Pacific Northwest, its Japanese parent in the mountains of Japan.
A yellow-flowered garden hybrid magnolia, not found wild; the yellow comes from the cucumbertree of eastern North America.
A yellow-flowered garden hybrid magnolia, not found wild; the yellow comes from the cucumbertree of eastern North America.
A yellow-flowered garden hybrid magnolia, not found wild; the yellow comes from the cucumbertree of eastern North America.
A garden hybrid magnolia, not found wild. Its parents are Asian magnolias.
A yellow-flowered garden hybrid magnolia, not found wild; the yellow comes from the cucumbertree of eastern North America.
A garden hybrid of star and lily magnolia, not found wild.
A yellow-flowered garden hybrid magnolia, not found wild; the yellow comes from the cucumbertree of eastern North America.
A garden selection of birch, not found wild. Birches grow wild across the cool north of the Northern Hemisphere.

habitat: A fast-growing garden shrub. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, on almost any soil.
distribution: A garden selection of border forsythia, a hybrid raised in cultivation from two Chinese forsythias, weeping and greenstem forsythia; not found wild.
A garden selection of boxwood, not found wild. Boxwoods grow wild in Europe, Asia and Africa.
A garden elm bred from Asian elms for resistance to Dutch elm disease; not found wild.
A garden elm bred from Asian elms for resistance to Dutch elm disease; not found wild.
A hybrid of garden origin between downy and Allegheny serviceberry, both natives of eastern North America.
A garden selection of a hybrid, of garden origin, between downy and Allegheny serviceberry, both natives of eastern North America; not found wild.
A hybrid of English oak and the white oak of eastern North America. The tree planted here is a narrow garden selection of it, not found wild.
A garden crabapple of uncertain parentage, not found wild.
A garden crabapple, not found wild. Crabapples grow wild across the temperate Northern Hemisphere.
A garden crabapple raised at the University of Illinois, not found wild.
A garden selection of a hybrid of bur oak and English oak, not found wild. Bur oak grows wild across central and eastern North America.

habitat: Open mountain forests, thickets and disturbed woodland. Planted, it does well in sun, part shade or dappled light, in acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild in Japan, and also in Korea and China.

habitat: Swamp forest on young alluvial soils, along rivers and in mixed forests; much of that habitat has been lost to rice fields.
distribution: Wild in northeast Asia: Japan, Korea, northeastern China and the Russian Far East.

habitat: Mixed mountain forests. It is grown as an ornamental tree.
distribution: Wild in northeastern China, Korea and the Russian Far East.

habitat: Near small rivers, bogs, springs and wet ground at the foot of mountains, mostly between about 2,500 and 5,000 feet. Planted, it takes sun or part shade and almost any soil, wet or dry.
distribution: Wild in northeast Asia: Japan, Korea, Manchuria, Siberia and the Russian Far East.

habitat: Where its parents, rowan and whitebeam, grow together; rare in the wild.
distribution: A natural hybrid of whitebeam and rowan, found at scattered places across much of Europe, from Britain and Ireland to Germany, Austria, Hungary and Romania, and in Turkey.

habitat: Dry slopes and river valleys.
distribution: Wild in eastern Europe and western Asia, including southern Russia, Turkey, Armenia and Iran.
A garden hybrid alder, not found wild.

habitat: A medium-sized tree with a dome-shaped crown and stout, level branches.
distribution: Swedish whitebeam, a natural hybrid of rowan, wild service tree and a whitebeam: native to southern Sweden, with scattered wild stands in Estonia, Latvia, Bornholm in Denmark, the far southwest of Finland and northern Poland, and found in England.

habitat: A whitebeam with lobed, oak-like leaves, hence its other name, oakleaf mountain ash.
distribution: Finnish whitebeam, a natural hybrid of rowan and a whitebeam: native to Norway, eastern Sweden and southwestern Finland, and locally in Latvia.
A garden hybrid of English oak and swamp white oak, not found wild.

habitat: A garden shrub. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, on well-drained soil, and stands occasional wet or dry spells.
distribution: A garden selection of rose of Sharon, not found wild. The species is native to east Asia, in southern China and Taiwan.

habitat: A garden shrub. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, on well-drained soil, and stands occasional wet or dry spells.
distribution: A garden selection of rose of Sharon, not found wild. The species is native to east Asia, in southern China and Taiwan.

habitat: Mountain thickets and rocky slopes. Planted as a low groundcover, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained loam, and tolerates poor soil, drought and pollution.
distribution: Wild in western China.
A garden selection of black mulberry, not found wild. Black mulberry has been grown so long in western Asia that its wild home is uncertain.

habitat: A garden fruit. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in well-drained, acid soil.
distribution: A garden selection of red raspberry, not found wild. The species grows wild across Europe and northern Asia, and its American variety across much of North America.

habitat: Usually dry places: ravines, thickets, ditches and forest edges in the mountains.
distribution: Wild in western China, in Gansu, Shaanxi, Sichuan and Tibet.

habitat: A garden shrub, grown for its layered branches and flat white spring flowers. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: A garden selection of doublefile viburnum, not found wild. The species grows wild in China, Korea and Japan.
A garden selection of a lilac collected in Korea, not found wild. The species grows wild in Korea and northern China.
A garden hybrid rhododendron raised in Massachusetts for cold hardiness, not found wild.
A garden hybrid azalea bred for cold hardiness, not found wild.

habitat: An understory tree of swamps, bogs, wet woods, lowlands and thickets, often growing in clumps. Planted, it does well in sun, part shade or dappled light, on moist soil.
distribution: Wild in eastern North America, mostly near the Atlantic coast, from Newfoundland south to Alabama.

habitat: Swamps, wetlands and stream banks, on wet soils, where it spreads slowly by runners into thickets.
distribution: Speckled alder, the North American form of grey alder: much of Canada below the tree line, and the northeastern United States, Vermont included. The species grows across the cooler parts of the Northern Hemisphere.
A thornless garden blackberry raised by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, not found wild.

habitat: A slow-growing evergreen garden shrub. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained, acid soil.
distribution: A garden hybrid of Japanese pieris and the mountain andromeda, Pieris floribunda, of the southern Appalachians, not found wild.

habitat: A garden tree. Planted, it does best in full sun to part shade, in moist, well-drained soil of average fertility.
distribution: A weeping garden form of Higan cherry, grown in Japan for centuries and not found wild.

habitat: A clumping ornamental grass. Planted, it grows in sun or part shade on almost any soil, wet or dry; the species seeds itself into the wild and is a problem plant in places.
distribution: A garden selection of Chinese silver grass, not found wild. The species grows wild in eastern Asia.

habitat: A clumping ornamental grass. Planted, it grows in sun or part shade on almost any soil, wet or dry; the species seeds itself into the wild and is a problem plant in places.
distribution: A garden selection of Chinese silver grass, not found wild. The species grows wild in eastern Asia.

habitat: A cool-season ornamental grass, named Perennial Plant of the Year in 2001. Planted, it does best in sun or part shade, on moist, well-drained soil.
distribution: A hybrid of two widespread Eurasian reed grasses, occasionally found wild in Europe and Asia. 'Karl Foerster' is a garden selection of it, found and introduced by the German nurseryman it is named for.

habitat: The species grows in shady woods; planted, it wants shade or dappled light and acid soil that stays moist.
distribution: A garden selection of autumn fern, not found wild. The species grows wild in eastern Asia, in China and Japan.
A garden hybrid of Mongolian and littleleaf linden, not found wild.
